outcome: Nothing found since 26 January 2024 settles or moves whether every prime appears in the first (least-prime-factor) Euclid–Mullin sequence; the one in-window item on this family, Booker and Simon's arXiv:2601.21901 (29 January 2026), treats analogues of the second (largest-prime-factor) sequence in residue classes and states that for the first sequence 'both of Mullin's questions remain open'.
problem_asks: One question, written from the statement alone. Let the Euclid–Mullin sequence be the sequence (OEIS A000945) with a(1) = 2 and a(n+1) = the least prime factor of 1 + a(1)·…·a(n). Part 1 (the only part): for every prime p (including 2), does there exist n with a(n) = p? The statement does not ask (i) whether membership is decidable, which is Mullin's companion question and is asked in the literature but not in this bullet; (ii) anything about the largest-prime-factor sequence; (iii) whether some Euclid-type sequence contains every prime, which is a broader question the literature also records as open. Those are noted as scope, not as parts of the bullet.

events.what_happened: Albert A. Mullin posed the question in 'Recursive function theory', Bulletin of the AMS 69 (1963), p. 737 (cited by Booker and Simon 2026 as reference [10]; one search snippet calls it Research Problem 8). Asked whether every prime occurs in the sequence and whether membership is recursive. The 1963 paper itself was not opened; the citation was read in Booker and Simon's bibliography.
events.delivers: Nothing established. It is the posing of the question.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, and the decidability question.
events.time_since_posted: Not applicable: a question, not a claim. Posed 1963; later papers still list it as open.
events.direction: No direction; it is a question. The only sources read record no expectation from Mullin.

events.what_happened: C. D. Cox and A. J. van der Poorten, 'On a sequence of prime numbers', J. Austral. Math. Soc. 8 (1968) 571–574 (per Booker and Simon's bibliography, not opened). Concerns Mullin's second sequence (largest prime factor). Booker and Simon 2026 (footnote 1) report that they showed all primes below 47 are omitted apart from the early terms 2, 3, 7, 43, and that they also claimed 47 is omitted, which was a numerical error (identified by Thorkil Naur) that went unnoticed for decades.
events.delivers: Second sequence only: omission of the primes below 47, apart from the early terms, plus a wrong claim about 47. Nothing about the first sequence.
events.remains: All of problem_asks for the first sequence.
events.time_since_posted: Not applicable (1968). The 47 claim was corrected in Booker and Simon 2026.
events.doubts: The claim that 47 is omitted is wrong (numerical error, per Booker and Simon 2026 footnote 1). Ruling out 47 became possible only with Wagstaff's computation of the 12th term in 1991, as stated there.
events.direction: For the second sequence: consistent with the later theorem that it omits infinitely many primes. No bearing on the first sequence.
people: Thorkil Naur (identified the error, per Booker and Simon 2026)

events.what_happened: T. Naur, 'Mullin's sequence of primes is not monotonic', Proc. AMS 90(1) (1984) 43–44 (per Booker and Simon's bibliography and Wikipedia's citation). Wikipedia cites it for non-monotonicity of the second sequence. Not opened.
events.delivers: Non-monotonicity of Mullin's second sequence, per Wikipedia. Says nothing about whether every prime occurs in the first sequence.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.time_since_posted: Not applicable (1984).
events.direction: No direction on the question.

events.what_happened: D. Shanks, 'Euclid's primes', Bull. Inst. Combin. Appl. 1 (1991) 33–36 (per Booker and Simon's bibliography; not opened). Gives the heuristic that the first sequence contains every prime: if a prime q were never a term, the partial products would have to avoid the class −1 mod q for all large n, which is implausible if they behave randomly among the invertible classes. Booker 2016 calls it 'a compelling heuristic argument of Shanks'. Not a proof.
events.delivers: A heuristic for the answer yes. It establishes no membership of any prime and proves nothing about the sequence.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.time_since_posted: Not applicable (1991). Heuristic still described as unproven in 2026 (Booker and Simon 2026).
events.doubts: Kurokawa and Satoh (2008) prove that the same heuristic fails in some explicitly characterised cases of the polynomial analogue over F_p[x], and their numerics support the analogue only outside those cases. This is about an analogue, not the integers, but it is the one known check of the reasoning's reliability and it is not a check of the integer case.
events.direction: Toward 'yes': every prime appears. Heuristic only.

events.what_happened: S. S. Wagstaff, Jr., 'Computing Euclid's primes', Bull. Inst. Combin. Appl. 8 (1993) 23–32 (per Booker and Simon's bibliography; not opened). Per an OEIS A000945 search snippet, Wagstaff computed the sequence through the 43rd term. Not opened.
events.delivers: Computation of early terms of the first sequence. Establishes no membership beyond the terms listed and says nothing about whether every prime appears.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.time_since_posted: Not applicable (1993).
events.directly_checkable: The listed terms can be checked by factoring 1 + the product of the earlier terms; the 44th term needs a 180-digit number factored.
events.direction: No direction on the question.

events.what_happened: Carl Pomerance's variant of Euclid's construction, cited by Booker 2016 as 'due to Pomerance' and given in Crandall and Pomerance, Prime Numbers: A Computational Perspective, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2005), §1.1.3 (book; not opened). Booker 2016 reports that one obtains a sequence containing every prime, with p_k the k-th smallest prime for k ≥ 5, and calls it a specific sequence containing every prime. A search snippet of Wooley's 2016 note (not opened) describes the construction as taking the least prime dividing d + 1 for a divisor d of the product of earlier terms. The date is the cited edition; an earlier edition may carry it. This is a variant, not Mullin's rule.
events.delivers: A different selection rule, claimed to contain every prime, and a different sequence from the least-prime-factor rule in the statement. It bears on the question only as a variant. The claim is reported second-hand; the proof was not read.
events.remains: The original first sequence (all of problem_asks for that sequence).
events.time_since_posted: Not applicable (2005 cited edition).
events.doubts: Proof not read. Booker's arXiv abstract (search snippet) describes the Pomerance variant as 'unpublished, but see [§1.1.3]', while the JIS version cites the book; this discrepancy is unresolved. The construction summary comes from a search snippet of Wooley's note.
events.direction: Variant only: if the reported claim holds, it contains every prime for a different sequence. No bearing on the statement's sequence.

events.what_happened: N. Kurokawa and T. Satoh, 'Euclid prime sequences over unique factorization domains', Experimental Mathematics 17(2) (2008) 145–152. Project Euclid lists first availability 19 November 2008. Reformulates the question in polynomial rings over finite fields (F_p[x]); proves that Shanks's argument fails in some explicitly characterised cases; numerics suggest Shanks's conjecture holds for the analogue outside those cases. Read from the Project Euclid abstract summary; the full text was not read.
events.delivers: An analogue over F_p[x], not the integers: the heuristic fails for some explicit cases of the analogue. It does not settle the integer question.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.

events.direction: Against the reliability of Shanks's heuristic in some cases of the analogue; supports the analogue elsewhere. No direction for the integer problem.

events.what_happened: Extensions of the computed terms of the first sequence, recorded in OEIS A000945. T. D. Noe's comment of 15 October 2010 reports Wilfrid Keller's GNFS factorisation (dated 9 March 2010 in the comment) of a(1)…a(43) + 1, giving the 44th term. The OEIS b-file runs to n = 51 (first 47 terms credited to T. D. Noe). Wikipedia says 51 terms are known 'as of September 2012'.

events.what_happened: A. R. Booker and S. A. Irvine, 'The Euclid–Mullin graph', arXiv:1508.03039 (v1 12 August 2015; v2 6 March 2016), J. Number Theory 165 (2016) 30–57 (journal details from a search snippet; DOI 10.1016/j.jnt.2016.01.013 on the arXiv page). The graph encodes every instance of Euclid's proof (branching over all prime factors at each step); the authors prove it is not a tree and study its structure theoretically and numerically. events.what_happened: A. R. Booker, 'A variant of the Euclid–Mullin sequence containing every prime', arXiv:1605.08929 (submitted 28 May 2016), J. Integer Sequences 19 (2016), Article 16.6.4 (published 4 July 2016 per the JIS page). Generalises Euclid's proof: iteratively choose a set I and a prime p_{k+1} dividing N_I. Theorem: for any finite set P of primes there is a generalised Euclid sequence with seed P containing every prime. The proof selects primes dividing d + n/d for divisors d of n. The paper says the original Euclid–Mullin question remains open and that 'even the broader question of whether there is any Euclid sequence containing every prime number remains open'. Read from the JIS HTML and the TeX source.
events.revisions: Single arXiv version. Journal version received 26 May 2016, revised 16 and 17 June 2016, published 4 July 2016.
events.delivers: Variants (generalised Euclid sequences with arbitrary finite seed and a modified choice rule) provably contain every prime. It does not settle the original sequence, which the paper itself calls open.
events.remains: The original first sequence (all of problem_asks). The paper's own words: the broader question also remains open.
events.time_since_posted: About 10 years.
events.direction: For variants: yes, every prime appears. For the original sequence: no result; the paper leaves it open.

events.what_happened: T. D. Wooley, 'A superpowered Euclidean prime generator', arXiv:1607.05267 (17 July 2016), Amer. Math. Monthly 124(4) (2017) 351–352 (per the arXiv comment). For k > 1 and n the product of the smallest k primes, the (k+1)-st prime is the least divisor exceeding 1 of n^(n^n) − 1. The abstract does not mention the Euclid–Mullin sequence.
events.delivers: A different generator (a deterministic next-prime rule). It does not address the Euclid–Mullin membership question.

events.what_happened: A. R. Booker and C. Pomerance, 'Squarefree smooth numbers and Euclidean prime generators', arXiv:1607.01557 (v1 6 July 2016; v2 7 July 2016; v3 8 Nov 2016; v4 10 Apr 2017), to appear in Proc. AMS (published 2017, vol. 145 no. 12, per an AMS listing seen in a search result; not opened). Shows that for prime p > 7 every residue mod p is represented by a squarefree number with largest prime factor at most p, and that y = p is best possible. Gives two applications to recursive prime generators: Corollary 7 (starting 2, 3, 7, 5, then the primes in order) and Corollary 8, which gives a sequence containing every prime. Section 6 poses whether the least-prime-choice sequence from Corollary 8 contains every prime. The heuristic counting argument (2^π(p) squarefree p-smooth integers against p classes mod p) suggests the answer is yes for large p. A footnote says at least one author thinks Mullin's decidability question is likely undecidable.
events.revisions: v2 7 Jul 2016; v3 8 Nov 2016; v4 10 Apr 2017 (the version read).
events.delivers: A residue-class covering result and two Euclid-type generators, one yielding a sequence containing every prime. The §6 question concerns the least-prime-choice variant of Corollary 8, not Mullin's rule as stated. The paper does not claim to settle Mullin's sequence and describes it as open with heuristic support for yes.
events.remains: The original first sequence (all of problem_asks), and the §6 least-prime variant.

events.what_happened: A. R. Booker and O. Simon, 'A generalisation of the Euclid–Mullin sequences', arXiv:2601.21901 (v1 29 January 2026; v2 2 February 2026; arXiv comment field '15 pages'). Extends Mullin's constructions to choose primes in residue classes, using sequences generated by cyclotomic polynomials Φ_m(cx). Main results concern the second-type (largest-prime) analogues. Theorem 1.6 (assuming ERH) and Theorem 1.7 (unconditional for m in {1,…,10,12,14,18}, with conditions on c) show the analogue omits infinitely many primes ≡ 1 mod m. Theorem 1.8 (unconditional, m a power of 2 greater than 2) gives an explicit omitted prime, showing at least one prime is omitted for infinitely many m. Conjecture 1.3 (generalised Euclid–Mullin) has parts (i) an f whose first-type sequence contains every prime ≡ a mod m, and (ii) second-type sequences omit infinitely many primes ≡ a mod m. The paper says it makes progress only on (ii), partly conditionally for m in {1, 2}. Its introduction states: 'As for the first sequence, both of Mullin's questions remain open, and very little is known.' Footnote 1 corrects Cox and van der Poorten's claimed omission of 47.
events.revisions: v1 29 Jan 2026 (20 KB); v2 2 Feb 2026 (21 KB, current). The change between versions was not compared.
events.delivers: For second-type analogues in residue classes ≡ 1 mod m: infinitely many primes omitted under ERH (Theorem 1.6), unconditionally for the listed moduli with conditions on c (Theorem 1.7), and at least one omitted prime for infinitely many m (Theorem 1.8). It does not touch the first sequence, which the paper itself describes as open. It gives no result on Conjecture 1.3(i), the residue-class analogue of 'every prime appears'.
events.remains: For the statement: all of problem_asks, by the paper's own statement. Also Conjecture 1.3(i) and the decidability question.

This is explicit: the omitted prime is identified by a stated rule. These are cyclotomic second-type sequences, not the first Euclid–Mullin sequence.

disputes.summary: Cox and van der Poorten (1968) claimed 47 is omitted from the second (largest-prime-factor) sequence. Booker and Simon (2026, footnote 1) report that this was a numerical error, identified by Thorkil Naur and unnoticed for decades; the exclusion of 47 became possible with Wagstaff's 12th-term computation in 1991. This concerns the second sequence only.

Booker's 2016 JIS paper credits Pomerance's variant to Crandall and Pomerance (2005, §1.1.3) and does not call it unpublished. A search snippet of the arXiv version (1605.08929) reads 'unpublished, but see [4, §1.1.3]'. The JIS TeX was read; the snippet was not opened. The discrepancy is unresolved and may be a version difference.

summary: Nothing in the sources read establishes or moves the answer to whether every prime appears in the first Euclid–Mullin sequence, and nothing in-window has done so. The only in-window item on the family is Booker and Simon's arXiv:2601.21901 (v1 29 January 2026), which I read in its v2 HTML. It works on analogues of the second (largest-prime-factor) sequence in residue classes; its main theorems are conditional on ERH in general and unconditional only for listed moduli, and it gives an explicit omitted prime for power-of-two moduli. Its introduction says 'As for the first sequence, both of Mullin's questions remain open, and very little is known,' and it makes no claim about the first sequence. Wikipedia's article (as fetched; last edited 8 June 2024 per the page) still lists the question as open, with 41 as the least prime not known to be a term, and does not mention the 2026 preprint. The OEIS A000945 entry (fetched in 2026) still asks the question and has no answer; its in-window comments (Spezia 2025, Hasler 2026) are maintenance. Two AI-related in-window items, AlphaProof Nexus (arXiv:2605.22763; 9 Erdős problems and 44 OEIS conjectures) and OEIS Open (arXiv:2608.11941; a 492-conjecture benchmark), touch OEIS conjectures in general. I checked the visible OEIS proof folders for AlphaProof Nexus and found no Euclid–Mullin IDs, but the folder listing is partial and the 492-conjecture list was not visible, so neither was verified against this problem. No source names an AI system in connection with this problem, and about 43 searches (including AI-specific ones naming Claude, GPT, Gemini and AlphaProof) found none. Older results fall into three groups. (1) Second-sequence results, which settle that infinitely many primes are missing from that sequence: Cox and van der Poorten (1968, with an erroneous claim about 47), Booker (2012), Pollack and Treviño (2014). (2) Variants, whose every-prime property is proved or claimed: Booker (2016, JIS), Booker and Pomerance (2016/2017), and Pomerance's variant (2005 book, claimed by Booker 2016, proof not read). (3) The heuristic for yes, Shanks (1991), which Kurokawa and Satoh (2008) show fails in some explicit cases of the F_p[x] analogue. Known term counts depend on snapshot: 43 (MathWorld), 47 (Programming Praxis), 51 (Rosetta Code; OEIS b-file to n = 51; Wikipedia 'as of September 2012'). Close calls: (a) Whether a variant counts for this bullet. I have treated the variants as variants: their own texts say the original sequence is open, and the bullet names Mullin's sequence. (b) Whether Booker–Simon's Theorem 1.8 (an explicit omitted prime) bears on the question. It concerns second-type cyclotomic sequences, so I treat it as not bearing. (c) Booker–Pomerance §6 poses an open question about the least-prime choice in their Corollary 8 construction; that is a variant, not Mullin's rule as written. Nothing in this record was checked against the Shanks 1991 paper or the Mullin 1963 paper; both are recorded from citations.
competing_reading: One could treat the variant results (Booker 2016; Booker and Pomerance 2016/2017; Pomerance's variant as reported) as partial answers to 'does every prime appear in a Euclid sequence', reading 'the Euclid–Mullin sequence' loosely. Against this, the bullet names Mullin's least-prime-factor sequence, and the papers that prove the variant results say the original question is open. A second reading treats Booker–Simon's Theorem 1.8, which names an omitted prime, as a 'no' direction for the problem. Against this, it omits primes from second-type cyclotomic sequences, not from the first sequence, so it cuts against neither answer for this bullet.
what_would_settle_it: For the question as stated: a proof that every prime is a term of A000945, or a proof that a specific prime is never a term, published or posted with full text. For the events: full texts of Shanks (1991), Mullin (1963), Cox and van der Poorten (1968), Naur (1984), Wagstaff (1993), Pollack and Treviño (2014) and the Pomerance chapter (Crandall–Pomerance §1.1.3) to check their content directly; the Stouthart (2024, Utrecht) thesis and the Simon (2024, Bristol) thesis to confirm they contain nothing about the first sequence; a journal version of Booker–Simon to see whether its first-sequence statement changed. For AI: the 492-conjecture list of OEIS Open, and the full AlphaProof Nexus OEIS folder listing with the 'View all files' link, to confirm that no Euclid–Mullin item is in either.
